Forage

/FOR-ij/ - rhymes with porridge · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Forage means to search around for food.

Black bears forage almost around the clock in late September, laying on the fat that will carry them through the den months.

Worked Example

The mushroom club's autumn walk has two rules and one ritual. Rule one: nothing goes in your basket until a guide has named it twice. Rule two: cut, don't pull, so the ground keeps its secret for next year. The ritual comes at noon, when forty people who have spent the morning stooping under pines compare baskets — and the retired pharmacist, as always, has quietly out-gathered everyone.

Forage is the exact word for what they are doing, because it means to search around for food — the looking is the heart of it. Nobody planted these chanterelles and no shelf holds them; the meal has to be found, patch by patch, which is why the verb belongs equally to bears in September and to people with baskets.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

rummage: To rummage is the same rooting around moved indoors — through drawers, bins, and glove boxes — and food is beside the point. To forage is to search the outdoors for something to eat: the two verbs share the hunting posture, but only forage puts a meal at the end.

glean: To glean is to gather what a harvest left behind — dropped ears of grain, missed apples — one narrow and tidy kind of food-searching. To forage is the wider verb: hunting out food wherever it grows wild, with no harvest required and no field to follow.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

cater: to bring the food in ready-made, no searching required

farm: to raise food on purpose in one place rather than go find it

Where it sits · how hard the next meal comes — graze → forage → scavenge

graze vs. forage: Grazing asks no search at all — the meal is the field underfoot, eaten where the animal stands — while to forage is to go looking, because nothing is waiting underfoot.

scavenge vs. forage: Scavenge goes past forage — the forager seeks out food where it grows; the scavenger lives on scraps, refuse, and whatever something else left behind.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — for-

Root — for-: fodder, animal feed (Old French feurre)

Suffix — -age

Suffix — -age: activity of

Put it together

Put it together: For- (fodder) + -age (activity of) = the activity of getting feed. Old French forrage was first a soldier's word: armies sent riders out to find feed for the horses, and to forage meant to scour the countryside for it. The military errand faded; the searching stayed.

Use the root in a new word: fodder

Use the root in a new word: fodder: Fodder is the root's plain-spoken cousin: the cut feed itself, stacked in the barn for animals that no longer have to look for it.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral

Forage is the naturalist's everyday verb, equally at home with bears, hens, and humans with baskets — the emphasis is always on searching. Keep it apart from this unit's migrate, which is about moving between regions, not hunting a meal: a herd migrates to the winter range, and then it forages there. For rooting through a junk drawer, rummage is the word; forage without food in view is a joke, and usually told as one.
